html:
The movement of Japanese contract workers to the sugar plantations of Hawaii, which began on a large scale in 1885. By 1920 people of Japanese descent made up about 43 percent of Hawaii's population, the largest group in the islands.

The Kingdom of Hawaii needed labour for its booming sugar estates, since disease had cut the native Hawaiian population. King Kalākaua visited Japan in 1881, and in 1885 the first ship of government sponsored migrants arrived with about 940 people. Japan, in the early years of the Meiji era, had many poor farmers ready to go. Tens of thousands followed on three year contracts, working long hours for low pay under harsh overseers.

Many stayed when their contracts ended. After the United States took Hawaii in 1898, men sent for brides from Japan through exchanged photographs, the "picture brides". The US Immigration Act of 1924 closed the door. Japanese Americans in Hawaii, unlike those on the mainland, were mostly not interned in World War II, and many served in the famous 442nd Regiment. Compare Indian indenture in other sugar colonies.
